title: Wall Contracts
evidence_status: Documented awards; reported access; disputed procurement
period: FY2026 obligations; 2026 lawsuit; historical access context labeled separately
summary: Fisher Sand & Gravel recorded $13.35 billion in FY2026 net federal contract obligations. Its family leadership and documented political access make the allocation of those contracts a concrete accountability question.

money.label: Net federal contract obligations
money.note: Commitments to the company; outlays are null in the captured response. Not personal income, profit or completed construction.

findings.label: Family business
findings.text: The company identifies founder Gene Fisher, his son and company president Tommy Fisher, and Tommy’s sons Grant and Ryan as successive generations involved in the business. Their economic stakes and distributions are not disclosed here.

findings.label: Procurement challenge
findings.text: Posillico, one of eleven prequalified contractors, filed a May 2026 protest alleging ten challenged task orders exceeded the underlying contract’s scope. It sought declarations and bid-preparation costs. These are a competitor’s claims, not findings of fraud.

findings.label: Concentration
findings.text: The Texas Tribune and ProPublica reported the lawsuit’s allegation that roughly 73% of the relevant contract value went to Fisher and Barnard. CBP defended the process as fair and based on qualifications and reasonable prices. Fisher and Barnard did not respond to those reporters.

findings.label: Reported access
findings.text: Trump and Kushner reportedly advocated for Fisher in 2019.
findings.period_scope: Historical context; before the financial window

findings.label: Wealth reporting
findings.text: Bloomberg described the Fishers as a new billionaire family in March 2026. The accessible excerpt establishes that reported characterization, but does not expose a reproducible valuation or individual ownership split. It is not treated as billions personally paid from contracts.
findings.evidence_status: Reported characterization; numeric valuation not reconstructed

counterevidence.text: A historical DoD Inspector General review found no evidence of undue influence in the records it examined for the 2019 Yuma 3 award. But restrictions on questions about White House communications prevented the auditors from fully resolving that issue. This limited finding concerns one earlier procurement, not all FY2026 awards.

analysis: The revealing pattern is a large concentration of awards to a politically connected family business, a specific procurement challenge and incomplete transparency around selection and delivery. Those facts support scrutiny of favoritism and value for money. They do not establish that Tommy Fisher personally received the contract total or that little construction proves fraud.
open_questions: Who approved the challenged scope changes and selection decisions, and what comparative bids support value for money?
For each award, what has been obligated, paid, subcontracted, delivered and accepted against its own timetable?
What are the family ownership percentages, company margins and actual distributions?
What contributions or lobbying expenditures can be linked to exact people and legal entities through dated FEC/LDA records?
publication_limits: Do not present aggregate national wall mileage as Fisher-specific completion.
Do not assert a current final disposition of the May 2026 lawsuit; later docket outcome was not independently established in this bounded review.
Do not claim campaign funds were recycled from these contracts without a traced money path.
Do not replace company obligations with personalcash or compute family profit using an assumed margin.
